question: Static directional (weathercock) stability requires that a sideslip β produces:

options.text: A yawing moment away from the relative wind
No yawing moment, since a sideslip creates no change in the fin's force in any case
A yawing moment that turns the nose into the relative wind (Cn_β > 0)

explanation: The fin, aft of the CG, generates side force from β that yaws the nose toward the oncoming flow, reducing β.

question: The fuselage contributes to directional stability:

options.text: Not at all, because the fuselage is fully symmetrical and produces no side force in any sideslip condition
Destabilisingly, since its side area ahead of the CG produces a yawing moment away from the wind

explanation: The forward fuselage in sideslip acts like a lifting body ahead of the CG, turning the nose further away.

question: A dorsal fin improves directional stability at large sideslip angles because:

options.text: It adds weight aft, which increases the aircraft's stability in every flight condition
It creates a vortex that delays fin stall, keeping the fin's side force rising

explanation: The low-aspect-ratio dorsal extension behaves like a strake, maintaining attached flow over the fin at high β.

question: Sweepback's effect on directional stability is:

options.text: Stabilising, since the forward-moving wing presents more span normal to the flow and more drag
Nil, since sweep only affects the lift of the wing and never the yawing moment, whatever the angle of sideslip

explanation: In sideslip the advancing swept wing has a smaller effective sweep, more lift and induced drag, yawing the nose back into the wind.

question: At very high angles of attack, directional stability can deteriorate because:

options.text: The CG moves forward, which pushes the centre of pressure ahead of the fin and so weakens directional stability
The fin is immersed in the fuselage and wing wake

explanation: Separated flow from the forebody and wing reduces the fin's effective dynamic pressure and lift slope.

question: Supersonic flight tends to reduce directional stability because:

options.text: The CG moves aft, since supersonic flight moves the centre of gravity behind the fin's own centre of pressure
The fin lift-curve slope decreases with Mach number above M 1

explanation: Supersonic lift slope ≈ 4/√(M² − 1) falls with M, so larger fins or ventral fins are needed.

question: Lateral static stability (dihedral effect) requires that a sideslip toward the lower wing produces:

options.text: A rolling moment that lowers it further
A rolling moment that raises the lower wing (Cl_β < 0)
No rolling moment, since the wings produce equal lift at any angle of sideslip

explanation: The aircraft sideslips toward the low wing; the dihedral effect rolls it back toward wings level.

question: Geometric dihedral provides lateral stability because in a sideslip:

options.text: The forward wing meets the airflow at a higher α and produces more lift
The CG moves toward the upper wing
The lower wing is heavier, which lowers its centre of gravity and so raises the stability of the aircraft

explanation: The sideslip velocity component has a normal component on each dihedral panel: up on the leading wing, down on the trailing wing.

question: A high-mounted wing contributes to lateral stability because:

options.text: Crossflow around the fuselage raises α at the root of the forward wing and lowers it at the trailing wing
The CG is lower, which is the main reason a high wing gives lateral stability, because the weight pulls the aircraft back to level

explanation: Flow deflected over the top of the fuselage in sideslip is upward at the windward root of a high wing, adding an effective dihedral of a few degrees. A low wing experiences the opposite.

question: Relative to a mid wing, a low-mounted wing requires:

options.text: More geometric dihedral, since its fuselage interference reduces the dihedral effect
Anhedral, which is the only geometric change that reduces the need for dihedral on any low wing

explanation: Fuselage crossflow reduces the leading wing's α at a low wing; designers add dihedral to compensate.

question: Sweepback provides a dihedral effect because:

options.text: The forward-moving wing has less effective sweep and more lift in a sideslip
It reduces span, which lowers the wing's moment of inertia and so improves lateral damping at all speeds

explanation: Lift ∝ cos²Λ_eff; sideslip reduces Λ on the leading wing and increases it on the trailing wing, rolling away from the sideslip.

question: High-wing swept transports often use anhedral because:

options.text: High wing position and sweep together would give excessive dihedral effect and poor Dutch roll damping
It reduces weight, since anhedral is lighter to build and so the wing needs less structure to carry the load

explanation: Anhedral reduces Cl_β to a balanced level relative to Cn_β.

question: The fin's side force in sideslip also produces a rolling moment because:

options.text: The fin's centre of pressure lies above the roll axis
It is aft of the CG
It is swept, which moves the fin's centre of pressure outboard and so produces a roll in every sideslip

explanation: Side force × height above the CG gives a rolling moment in the stabilising sense — part of the total dihedral effect.

question: Extending inboard flaps changes the dihedral effect:

options.text: It reduces it, because lift is concentrated near the root where the dihedral arm is small
It reverses it only in climbs

explanation: Rolling moments from sideslip act through the spanwise arm; inboard loading shortens it.

question: Dutch roll is:

options.text: A coupled oscillation in yaw and roll, with the wingtips tracing ellipses

explanation: Yaw produces sideslip; dihedral effect rolls the aircraft; the resulting sideslip and yaw reverse, and the cycle repeats out of phase.

question: Dutch roll tendency increases when:

options.text: Lateral stability (dihedral effect) is strong relative to directional stability
Directional stability is strong relative to lateral stability

explanation: A large Cl_β/Cn_β ratio amplifies the roll response to each yaw swing. Swept wings at high CL and high altitude are most prone.

question: Dutch roll damping decreases with altitude at constant EAS because:

options.text: Aerodynamic damping ∝ ρ·V ∝ √σ, while the restoring moments ∝ q are unchanged

explanation: At σ = 0.374, damping falls to 0.61 of its sea-level value relative to stiffness — yaw dampers are often required aloft.

question: The primary recovery input for a large Dutch roll with the yaw damper failed is:

options.text: Small, well-timed aileron inputs (or reducing altitude/speed per procedure), avoiding rudder that can amplify it

explanation: Out-of-phase rudder inputs easily reinforce the oscillation; aileron opposing the roll damps it. Lower altitude and moderate speed improve natural damping.

question: Increasing fin area generally:

options.text: Increases directional stability and yaw damping, reducing Dutch roll tendency but promoting spiral instability
Has no effect on spiral mode

explanation: Cn_β and Cn_r both rise; relative to Cl_β the directional side dominates, which slows spiral recovery.

question: Spiral instability occurs when:

options.text: Lateral stability is strong relative to directional stability
Directional stability is strong relative to lateral stability

explanation: In a slight bank the aircraft sideslips; a strong fin yaws it into the turn faster than dihedral effect can level it; the outer wing speeds up and bank increases.

question: A spirally unstable aircraft left with a small bank will:

options.text: Slowly increase bank and descend in a tightening spiral

explanation: The divergence is slow (time to double of tens of seconds) and easily corrected, but dangerous if unnoticed in cloud.

question: Designers accept mild spiral instability rather than strong Dutch roll because:

options.text: Dutch roll never occurs with a fin
Spiral divergence is slow and easily corrected, while poorly damped Dutch roll is objectionable and hard to control

explanation: The two modes pull in opposite directions through Cl_β/Cn_β; the compromise favours good Dutch roll damping.

question: Strong dihedral effect relative to directional stability gives:

options.text: Good spiral stability but a greater Dutch roll tendency
Poor spiral stability and no Dutch roll

explanation: It levels the wings quickly (spiral stable) but amplifies roll in response to yaw (Dutch roll).

question: Rolling produces sideslip toward the lower wing because:

options.text: The lift vector tilts, and the unbalanced horizontal component moves the aircraft sideways

explanation: Until a coordinated turn develops, the horizontal lift component accelerates the aircraft toward the low wing: sideslip, which triggers dihedral effect and weathercock yaw.

question: An aircraft with strong dihedral effect can be turned with rudder alone because:

options.text: Yaw produces sideslip, and the dihedral effect converts it into roll

explanation: Secondary effect of rudder: yaw → sideslip → roll via Cl_β, and the advancing wing's extra speed adds to it.

question: A yaw damper:

options.text: Senses yaw rate and applies rudder to oppose it, damping Dutch roll

explanation: It adds artificial Cn_r, especially valuable at high altitude where natural damping is weak.

question: A yaw damper includes a wash-out (high-pass) filter so that:

options.text: It works only on the ground
It damps oscillations but does not oppose the steady yaw rate of a coordinated turn

explanation: Steady yaw rate in a turn is intended; the filter removes the steady component and acts only on oscillatory yaw.

question: Flight with the yaw damper inoperative is often restricted to:

options.text: Lower altitudes and moderate speeds where natural Dutch roll damping is adequate

explanation: Natural damping ∝ √σ at constant EAS; descending restores it.

question: A skidding turn (ball displaced toward the outside of the turn) indicates:

options.text: Too much rudder for the bank angle; the nose is yawed toward the inside

explanation: The tail is thrown outward; correct by reducing rudder in the direction of turn (step on the ball).

question: A slipping turn (ball displaced toward the inside of the turn) indicates:

options.text: Too little rudder for the bank angle, or too much bank

explanation: The aircraft sideslips toward the low wing; add rudder toward the turn.

question: In a steady coordinated turn, the overbanking tendency at low speed is countered by:

options.text: Slight opposite aileron to hold bank

explanation: The outer wing's higher speed produces more lift; at low speed and in steep turns this exceeds lateral stability, requiring aileron against the turn.

question: An aircraft held in a steady sideslip with crossed controls has:

options.text: Aileron opposing the dihedral effect and rudder opposing weathercock stability

explanation: Dihedral effect tries to roll away from the slip; weathercocking tries to yaw into it. Both must be held.

question: Maximum sustainable sideslip angle (e.g. crosswind limit) is usually set by:

options.text: Available rudder authority or aileron authority to oppose dihedral effect

explanation: Either control may reach full deflection first; strong dihedral effect makes aileron the limit.

question: Lateral stability alone (without directional stability) cannot restore wings-level flight because:

options.text: It acts only through the sideslip that a bank produces, which also brings in directional effects

explanation: Rolling moment from Cl_β requires β; the aircraft's response combines roll and yaw in the spiral and Dutch roll modes.

question: A ventral fin or strakes below the tail are added to:

options.text: Maintain directional stability at high angles of attack or high Mach, where the upper fin loses effectiveness

explanation: Below the fuselage they remain in clean flow when the upper fin is blanketed at high α.

question: Directional divergence occurs when:

options.text: Cn_β < 0 — sideslip produces a yawing moment that increases it

explanation: Static directional instability; the aircraft yaws away from the relative wind.

question: Anhedral (negative dihedral) produces:

options.text: A destabilising contribution to lateral stability (Cl_β more positive)

explanation: The forward wing loses α in sideslip; used deliberately where other contributions (high wing, sweep) are excessive.

question: Dutch roll period and damping ratio are typically:

options.text: Fractions of a second and zero damping
A few seconds and moderate to light damping

explanation: The mode frequency comes from Cn_β stiffness about the yaw inertia; damping from Cn_r, reduced by adverse cross terms.

question: At high altitude, swept-wing transports have more Dutch roll tendency because:

options.text: Higher CL increases sweep dihedral effect while aerodynamic damping falls

explanation: Both factors push the Cl_β/Cn_β ratio and damping in the unfavourable direction.

question: Roll subsidence mode is:

options.text: A rapid, non-oscillatory convergence of roll rate after an aileron input or disturbance

explanation: Strong roll damping gives a first-order response with a short time constant.

question: Propeller slipstream affecting directional trim is caused by:

options.text: The spiralling slipstream striking the fin on one side

explanation: The rotating wake meets the fin at an angle, producing a side force and yaw that varies with power and speed.

question: A long fuselage forebody (e.g. a stretched aircraft) typically requires:

options.text: A larger fin to restore directional stability

explanation: More side area ahead of the CG is destabilising; the fin term V_V must increase.

question: After an engine failure in a twin, holding wings level with zero bank requires:

options.text: Rudder against the yaw and a sideslip toward the dead engine, with aileron against the dihedral roll

explanation: With no bank, the fin side force must be balanced by a sideslip-generated body side force; a small bank toward the live engine removes most of the sideslip.

question: Spiral stability can be improved by:

options.text: Increasing fin area and reducing dihedral
Increasing dihedral effect or reducing fin area

explanation: Raising Cl_β relative to Cn_β favours wings-levelling over turning into the sideslip.

question: Dutch roll can be reduced in design by:

options.text: Increasing fin area/yaw damping or reducing excessive dihedral effect

explanation: Lower Cl_β/Cn_β and higher Cn_r both help; hence anhedral on high swept wings and yaw dampers.

question: A high-wing aircraft compared with a low-wing aircraft of the same dihedral has:
explanation: Fuselage interference adds effective dihedral to a high wing and subtracts it from a low wing.

question: Pure rudder-induced yaw at constant speed initially produces, before any roll develops:

options.text: Sideslip and a side force; then roll toward the yaw

explanation: The aircraft's inertia keeps its flight path while the nose yaws; β creates side force and, through Cl_β, roll.

question: Turn coordination in fly-by-wire systems commonly:

options.text: Adds rudder automatically to cancel sideslip during rolling

explanation: Feedback of lateral acceleration or β drives the rudder to keep the ball centred.

question: An aircraft whose fin stalls at large sideslip may show:

options.text: Rudder lock or directional divergence, with the rudder floating to full deflection

explanation: Beyond fin stall the restoring moment collapses; on reversible controls, hinge moments can drive the rudder to its stop. Dorsal fins help.

question: Wingtip devices raised well above the wing (winglets) affect lateral stability by:

options.text: Adding a dihedral-like contribution from their side force above the roll axis

explanation: In sideslip winglets produce side forces acting above the CG, generating a stabilising rolling moment.

question: The spiral mode is:

options.text: Oscillatory with a period of seconds
Non-oscillatory: a slow convergence or divergence in bank and heading

explanation: It is a first-order mode; its time constant depends on the balance of Cl_β, Cn_β and damping.

question: In a correctly coordinated turn, the slip ball is centred because:

options.text: The resultant of gravity and centripetal acceleration lies along the aircraft's vertical axis
There is no side force on any surface

explanation: Coordination aligns the apparent gravity vector with the aircraft's normal axis: zero lateral acceleration.

question: When the aircraft rolls into a bank without rudder, the initial yaw is:

options.text: Away from the turn (adverse yaw), from ailerons and roll-rate effects

explanation: Both aileron drag difference and roll-rate lift tilt give adverse yaw; rudder coordination is needed.

question: Directional stability in a steep climb at low speed with high power is often reduced because:

options.text: Propeller normal force ahead of the CG and slipstream effects on the fin act destabilisingly

explanation: A propeller disc at yaw produces side force ahead of the CG; asymmetric slipstream alters fin flow.
